text: Then they chose the wrong door.
speaker: Enhedu

text: They spent the better part of an hour on the brackets. The bronze had been driven deep and sealed with something harder than ordinary mortar. Balag worked the iron tools. Enhedu searched the masonry for weak points. Zik checked every inch of the entrance for traps while Kurash stood off to the side, shifting his weight and asking twice whether they were certain anything waited on the other side. Zik told him yes. The door opened with a long scream of metal that traveled down the passage and came back altered. Torchlight spilled into the chamber beyond.
speaker: Narrator

text: Zik held everyone at the threshold while he read the room from the doorway. The jamb carried no soot above shoulder height, which meant no ordinary lamp had burned here after the chamber was sealed. A faint gray bloom clung to the lower stones instead. He scraped it with the tip of the awl and rubbed the powder between finger and thumb. Salt, but not the loose desert salt that crept into abandoned masonry. This had risen through the wall from below, drawn upward by water that should not have existed at this depth.
speaker: Narrator

text: The floor had settled less than a finger's breadth toward the throne. Every line of gold followed that fall. Plates overlapped cups at measured intervals; chains bridged the narrow gaps; coins filled the spaces between them. It was a complete surface disguised as treasure. Zik pointed out the darker squares where the weight changed and made Kurash repeat the warning back to him. Kurash did, impatiently, his eyes never leaving the nearest bowl. Balag tested the lintel with the iron bar. Enhedu studied the seams rather than the wealth.
speaker: Narrator

text: There was dust everywhere else. It lay thick along the walls, packed into the throne's carvings, soft enough on the untouched border of the floor to preserve the smallest disturbance. The treasure itself remained clean.

text: Zik replied. The torch flames stood straight. He could hear each man's breathing and, beneath it, a faint mineral tick from somewhere under the black paving.

text: Nothing crosses that pattern until I know what it does.

text: Kurash nodded. The answer came easily. Believing it was another matter. Gold covered the floor in careful geometric lines across black stone—plates, cups, coins, small statues, chains, jewelry—the wealth of a kingdom arranged with such deliberate care that the hoard looked less like an offering and more like a mechanism left waiting. No one moved at first. Balag stayed where he was. Enhedu's eyes narrowed. Kurash made a sound that almost became a laugh.

text: Because no one buries a room like this and walks away without leaving something behind to guard it.

text: Then the trap is still here.
speaker: Zik

text: Kurash's expression shifted. Zik watched the calculation happen behind his eyes. The boy no longer saw a warning. He saw a house. A horse. A woman. A life that no longer required following another man's orders. Zik knew that look. He had believed the same things once.

text: The young man moved anyway. He crossed the threshold and closed his hand around a heavy golden bowl. The pattern on the floor broke. A single tile sank under his foot. For one heartbeat nothing happened. Then the ceiling opened. The stone slab dropped with perfect, silent speed. It caught Kurash below the ribs and drove him into the floor. His scream lasted less than a second. The slab pinned him across the gold. Blood spread in a dark sheet between the coins and over the curve of the bowl still trapped in his hand.
speaker: Narrator
note: Death beat. Do not rush the final sentence.

text: No one spoke. Balag took one step forward, hand reaching toward the body as if he could pull the moment back. Enhedu stood motionless, knife still under her arm, face unreadable. The blood reached the edge of a coin and kept going. Zik's share of the room had just grown by one. The first thought that arrived was practical: one less share. The second was that he hated himself for thinking it. The second thought lasted longer.
speaker: Narrator
note: Aftershock. Cold, controlled narration.

speaker: Narrator
note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

speaker: Narrator
note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

text: Zik stepped around the body and entered the chamber. The treasure had been arranged around a central path. The pattern itself made the trap obvious once it had sprung. Whoever built the room had not wanted to keep people out. They had wanted to control the way people came in.
speaker: Narrator

text: At the far end a stone throne rose from the floor. A skeleton sat upon it, wrapped in the last scraps of royal robes so old they seemed to cling to the bones only because they had forgotten how to fall away. A crown of blackened silver rested on the skull. At its center sat the same spiral and drop. Zik had seen versions of that mark before. It appeared on private seals belonging to kings whose reigns ended short and incomplete. Some vanished. Others were erased from monuments so thoroughly that later scholars argued over whether they had ever existed. He had always called it politics. Now he was less certain.
speaker: Narrator

text: A leather-bound journal rested in the skeleton's lap. Beside it lay a small brass compass. The torchlight caught the compass and threw a dull gleam across its face. He knew it. He had watched his father carry that same compass through most of his childhood—the worn leather case, the dent along the rim, the tiny scratch across the glass. His father had been carrying it the day he disappeared. Something in Zik's chest pulled tight, sharp and unexpected. For a moment the chamber seemed too small. He forced the breath out slowly and crossed the room.
speaker: Narrator
Narrator
note: Short attribution/action beat; keep tight to surrounding dialogue.

text: He ignored the warning. The compass lay clean amid the dust, as if the years had simply refused to touch it. When he picked it up the metal was cold enough to hurt. The needle spun once, then twice, then settled. It pointed straight down. He stood there longer than he meant to, turning the compass once in his hand, before he told himself the instrument was broken and opened the journal. The leather was cracked and dark with age, but the binding still held. The last page was already waiting. Two lines stood in his father's hand:
speaker: Narrator

text: IF YOU FIND THIS, DO NOT LOOK FOR ME.
speaker: Bel-iddin
note: Read as Bel-iddin's written warning, firm and deliberate.

speaker: Bel-iddin
note: Read as Bel-iddin's written warning, firm and deliberate.

text: A third line had been added beneath in different ink. The handwriting was uneven, the letters pressed so hard the pen had nearly torn the page.

text: ZIKIR—WHATEVER YOU DO, DO NOT OPEN THE SECOND DOOR.
speaker: Bel-iddin

text: The words sat there. Zik read them twice. The chamber stayed quiet around him. Then the torch flame bent sideways. The shadows on the walls were moving, and not with the fire. The skeleton's jaw shifted. Balag swore under his breath. Enhedu's knife was in her hand before the sound finished leaving his mouth. The empty sockets of the skull turned toward Zik.

text: Then the skeleton collapsed. Bones struck stone. Dust rose from the throne and rolled across the floor. Zik stumbled back, journal clutched to his chest, as the chamber trembled under their feet. Something far below the tomb shifted—slow, massive, almost gentle, like a sleeper turning over beneath the earth. Zik closed the journal. The sound echoed through the chamber.
